name: Slate grey
lede: Slate grey is the dark blue-tinted grey of roofing slate, a name that painters, paint makers and fieldworkers have all used loosely.

sections.title: A stone's color
sections.body: Slate is a metamorphosed mudstone or shale that splits cleanly into thin sheets for roof tiles [1]. The Pigment Compendium stresses that the word names no specific mineral, because the composition depends on the local mudstone [1]. The color word follows the stone: Paterson defines slate grey as the color of grey slate, a dark grey, and lists the web color SlateGray (#708090) as one of the 140 X11 colors [2]. The swatch is Ridgway's of 1886 and also appears in ISCC-NBS 1955 and Maerz and Paul 1930 [3]. Neighbors in the library include [[payne-s-grey]], [[dark-slate-grey]] and [[davy-s-grey]] [3].

sections.title: Slate in the paint box
sections.body: Slate was ground up as a material. Heaton, writing in 1928, records slate powder sold in grades of different fineness and used in the paint trade as an inert filler for stopping and filling compounds for woodwork and machinery [1]. A slate black was made by calcining bituminous shale, and Mayer's phrase for it is a shale black containing 15 per cent carbon [4]. Slate white is only an old name for lead white [4]. A further "slate blue" in the same sources was a pale artificial ultramarine in the 1920s [4].

sections.title: Grey that hides a goat
sections.body: Finlay records a field use. In Ladakh a guide explains that the animals the author cannot see are neither blue nor sheep but slate grey, halfway between sheep and goats, and the author finds them only when pale legs show against orange rock [5]. The scene shows how well a grey animal vanishes against a grey scree slope.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, slate grey appears in 485 paintings, 2.04 per cent, as photographed, more than 69 per cent of the named colors [6]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 1.9 times the expected rate [6]. [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]] uses it most, 5 of 287 works here, but no painter stands out against the museum baseline [6]. It is over-represented in India, 2.3 times expected [6]. In printed English the word peaks in the 1940s, and rose fastest in the 2000s [7]. A color match in an aged photograph is not a pigment test [6].
